text: This chapter's functions still share one weakness: they only run when someone opens a console and types the command, or when a Scheduled Task on some VM fires. A closed laptop runs nothing, and a VM running a Scheduled Task has to stay on all day just to execute a two-minute script. Azure Automation runs the script inside Azure itself, on a managed schedule, with no server of your own required.

An Automation account is the Azure resource holding everything Azure Automation manages — runbooks, schedules, credentials. A runbook is the actual script imported into that account, and runbook types include PowerShell and Python, the same two languages this course teaches. New-AzAutomationAccount creates the account, Import-AzAutomationRunbook uploads a script as a draft runbook, and Publish-AzAutomationRunbook makes that draft the live version that's actually allowed to run.

The runbook's content is just PowerShell — the same filter-and-loop pattern from Lesson 6, now running inside Azure. The real difference is Connect-AzAccount -Identity: inside a runbook, Azure Automation signs in using the Automation account's own system-assigned managed identity, an identity Azure manages with no app ID and no client secret for the script to store or ever accidentally leak into a log.

A schedule is a separate Automation object, created once with New-AzAutomationSchedule and a start time and interval, then linked to a specific runbook with Register-AzAutomationScheduledRunbook. DayInterval 1 means every day. From that point on, the script runs inside Azure at the scheduled time every night, whether anyone's laptop happens to be open or not.

Three places this script could live, side by side: a laptop that's closed or asleep simply doesn't run it; a Scheduled Task needs its VM powered on 24 hours a day just in case, which fights directly against Chapter 6's own cost-savings automation; an Azure Automation runbook runs inside Azure's own infrastructure, on schedule, authenticated with a managed identity, with nothing of yours that has to stay running.

This closes out PowerShell for Azure automation. Next, Chapter 3 turns to Python for the same kind of work — the Azure SDK for Python, authenticating a Python script, and a real worked example of provisioning a resource, to see where Python earns its place alongside everything PowerShell has done so far.
